analysis.one_liner: Requires groups that fund political ads to disclose their identities and donors.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee after its June 2000 introduction, with 21 Republican cosponsors and no vote ever taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill required anyone who spends $10,000 or more a year on ads or other communications mentioning federal candidates or officeholders to put their name on the message, identify their officers, and list every donor who gave $1,000 or more toward the spending. Radio and TV ads would have had to carry a spoken 'responsible for the content' statement, and stations would have had to keep the sponsor's donor information available to the public. It was introduced in June 2000, sent to two House committees, and never moved again before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters watching campaign ads. Anyone who sees an ad attacking or supporting a candidate could find out who paid for it and who the major funders were — on the ad itself, on request, or on the sponsor's or station's website.

how_it_helps.text: Groups spending $10,000 or more a year on non-broadcast communications mentioning federal candidates or officeholders must include their name, address, and phone number (or website) in the communication and identify officers and donors of $1,000 or more on request or online [S3].

Broadcast ads mentioning federal candidates must carry a clearly spoken 'is responsible for the content of this advertisement' statement, and on TV the statement must also appear on screen for at least 4 seconds [S3].

Stations broadcasting covered ads must keep sponsor information, post it on their websites if they have one, and make it available for public inspection; the rules also extend to cable and satellite video distributors [S3].
Violations carry civil penalties of up to $5,000-$10,000 or a multiple of the amount spent, with possible criminal fines and up to one year imprisonment for knowing and willful violations [S3].
The requirements would have taken effect January 1, 2001, covering the 2002 election cycle onward [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Groups and donors that run election-related ads without wanting their funding revealed, and broadcast and cable stations, which must collect, retain, post, and answer requests for sponsor information. Issue-advocacy organizations and their large donors would either disclose or scale back spending.
analysis.who_pays_short: Anonymous ad funders and broadcast stations

drawbacks.text: Donor privacy: any person giving $1,000 or more to a group's ad campaign would be publicly identified with the amount, which critics of disclosure rules argue can expose supporters of unpopular causes to harassment [S3].
Broadcast stations face new paperwork: collecting sponsor and donor information, posting it online, and answering phone, email, and fax requests from the public [S3].

The bill is disclosure-only: it does not limit how much money can be spent or require reporting to a regulator of the spending itself, so groups could split spending among affiliates or stay under the $10,000 annual threshold to avoid it [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — voters knowing who is behind campaign ads — is real but indirect: it improves information rather than changing anyone's finances. The costs are modest and fall on ad-funding groups that want anonymity and on stations handling records. The bill's main weakness is that disclosure can be avoided by structuring spending under the $10,000 threshold, and it does nothing to cap the money itself. Still, the design is reasonable and the burden on ordinary people is essentially zero.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Administration and Commerce committees, then to a Commerce subcommittee, and neither committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Castle introduced the bill on June 9, 2000, joined by 14 original cosponsors including Reps. Shays and Leach, all Republicans [S3].
It was referred the same day to the Committee on House Administration and to the Committee on Commerce [S5].
On June 20, 2000, the Commerce Committee referred it to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection, where it stayed [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded for the bill, and the 106th Congress ended January 3, 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Groups that fund campaign ads anonymously, along with their large donors, since no disclosure requirement ever took effect; the committees that held the bill never had to act on it.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes, so no roll-call split exists; all 21 cosponsors and the sponsor were Republicans, and the bill died in committee without opposition ever being recorded.

industries.industry: Issue-advocacy groups and their large donors
industries.note: Anyone spending $10,000 or more a year on ads mentioning federal candidates would have had to name themselves, their officers, and every $1,000-plus funder, ending the ability to run election ads anonymously. Their spending would have been subject to civil and criminal penalties for hiding sponsorship [S3].

Stations would have had to collect sponsor and donor information, post it online, and make it available on request — a new compliance duty. The bill also struck 'radio station' and replaced it with 'broadcast station,' extending existing sponsor-identification rules to all broadcast outlets, and added cable and satellite distributors [S3].
